items.passage: I was a terrible liar at eleven. I remember the white crust of salt cracking under my sandals as I walked back, the fish cold against my ribs, my chest bright with something like triumph. Smell of cut grass and the harbor's salt,
and a ball thudding off the far goalpost.
Okja sits on the bleacher's lowest step,
her mother's medicine in a paper bag.

The boys kick it high, past the chalk line,
past the fence, toward the road to Seoul,
and every time it bounces back,
fetched by someone smaller, running home.

She has packed a bag twice this year.
Twice she has unpacked it by morning.

When the ball rolls to her shoes at last,
she holds it for a while, feels its weight,
then tosses it gently back onto the field.
The floodlights blink on, one bank at a time,
and gulls drift low across the stands.

items.passage: Why does a man wear a hat indoors? My daughter, Priya, asked this of Mayor Marlon one wet afternoon in the drying shed of the tea estate above Surabaya, where I had come, as the town's only doctor, to discuss the fever in the pickers' quarters. Marlon laughed and tipped the wide straw brim lower. He told me the clinic would get its new beds after the harvest, the same promise he had made after the last harvest. Each time I pressed him on the numbers, he adjusted the hat, and its shadow slid across his eyes like a shutter. Later, walking down between the rows, Priya said she thought he must have been cold. I told her yes, perhaps. But I had noticed that when the estate owner arrived in his car, Marlon took the hat off at once and held it against his chest, his face suddenly bare and eager.

items.passage: Three rules governed the old weaving house in Lisbon, and you learned them on your first day: no lamp after midnight, no cloth cut before it is finished, and no news spoken until it is certain. Rafaela, who had bought the house that winter, kept all three. Each morning she climbed to the loom room while Mateo, the gardener, pruned the lemon trees below, and each morning she wove one more row of a blue cloth with no pattern anyone could name. The ship carrying her brother was weeks overdue. When Mateo asked why she did not weave something useful, a shawl or a blanket, she only said that the cloth was not finished. Rows gathered like days. Once, when a rumor of a wreck came up the hill, her hands stopped above the threads for a full hour; then she tied the next knot and went on. By midsummer, Mateo had begun bringing her a sprig of lemon blossom each dawn and laying it, without a word, beside the growing blue.

items.passage: Night is honest. In the sanatorium above the lake outside Bergen, I learned that patients say at two in the morning what they hide by daylight. Thorvald, my night patient, could not sleep unless I wheeled him to the end of the dock, where the water lay black and still. On the fourth night he showed me an envelope addressed to his brother, sealed and stamped and eleven years old. He had written it the week after their quarrel. He never mailed it, he said, and his brother had died the following spring. He held it on his blanket while he talked, and I understood that the apology had become an anchor he dragged behind him, slowing every hour he had left. Before dawn he asked me, Sigrid, to keep it for him. I put it in my apron pocket, where it weighed almost nothing.

items.passage:
Who pays a clockmaker for the hours he gives away?
My father, Santiago, bent above his bench
on Forty-Third Street, where the trains shook dust
from the rafters into every open case.
Ottavio came in winter with a watch
his wife had worn, its mainspring broken, its glass
clouded like a frozen pond.
He counted out his nickels on the counter.
My father pushed them back without a word
and worked past closing, past supper, past the lamps,
spending his minutes like coins on a stranger
while I translated nothing, for nothing needed saying.
When the watch ticked, Ottavio wept in Italian.
My father answered him in Spanish.
I stood between them with my English,
the only one who thought words were required.

options: giving his own time freely in place of taking payment
wasting time carelessly on a repair he did not value
charging Ottavio for every minute of his labor

Who else still remembered that our grandmother had called the house Two Ravens? Yona and I were selling what was left of it at the Saturday market, spreading her blankets and tin cups across a folding table in the wind. We had argued that morning over a cracked mirror, and for an hour we spoke only to customers. Then a woman lifted the carved sign from the bottom of a crate and read the name aloud. Yona looked at me, and I felt the old ease of being twins rush back, the way we used to finish each other's sentences at her table. Neither of us would sell it. We wrapped it in her red blanket and set it under the table, between our feet. By noon dust had settled on everything, and the vendor beside us was packing up his melons.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall mood of the passage?
A) Strained tension that a shared memory eases only for a moment
B) Wistful affection that outlasts a brief strain between brothers
C) Quiet irritation between brothers forced to share a dull task
D) Cheerful excitement about bargaining with customers at market
### lit40-medium-01-030 — skill inferences · 유형 tone_or_mood · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 정서의 비중을 판단해야 하며, 오답은 정반대가 아니라 비중이 틀린 어조다
[지문]
By the time this reaches you, Abena, the cooperative will have finished sorting the dry-season seed. I have been given the cowpea jars, which you would find funny, since you once swore I could not tell one bean from another. Mother says you promised, before you left, that we would plant the back plot together when you came home. Neither of us can remember you saying it, and I worry a little that you will arrive and find that promise a stranger. Still, I have already set aside two jars with your name on them in my worst handwriting, and I keep picturing your hands in that red soil. Come soon. The jars are labeled. The neighbor's goats have learned to open our gate, so bring wire.

[질문] Which choice best describes the overall tone of the letter?
A) Anxious uncertainty about whether the promise was ever made
B) Hesitant doubt relieved by only occasional moments of hope
C) Hopeful warmth that carries a slight trace of uncertainty
D) Dutiful formality suited to reporting on the cooperative
### lit40-medium-01-031 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다
[지문]
I had soldered the same joint three times when Bogdan took the iron from my hand. 'Again,' he said, and set a cold radio in front of me. I wanted to tell him that no one fixes radios anymore, that I could be in Tel Aviv learning to code by now. Then I saw the folded letter under his ledger, an offer from a conservatory, dated forty years ago and never answered; my mother had told me he stayed to keep this shop open after my grandfather fell ill. I picked up the iron without arguing. When he leaned over to check my work, I tilted the lamp toward his side so he would not have to squint. Outside, a bus groaned up the hill toward the port.

[질문] Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Tamar and Bogdan?
A) Tamar feels only frustration with an elder who refuses to modernize.
B) Bogdan feels indebted to Tamar's family for the sacrifices they made.
C) Bogdan is a stern master who treats Tamar as a mere hired hand.

### lit40-medium-01-032 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다

Riccardo slid into the booth first, the way he always had back home, and ordered for both of them without asking. Koa let him. When the waitress brought pancakes instead of the eggs Riccardo had insisted Koa liked, Koa noticed the mix-up before anyone else and quietly cut into the stack as if he had wanted it all along. Earlier, on the drive in, Riccardo had admitted that nobody at his new school knew his name yet, and had laughed too loudly afterward. So Koa praised the syrup, asked for a second pot of coffee, and stayed until Riccardo stopped checking his phone. ### lit40-medium-01-033 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다
[지문]
Nobody sleeps in this room. SALMA, sixteen, sits beside RASHID, an old friend of her father's, under a buzzing light.
SALMA: The car was blue. I saw it.
RASHID: I saw gray. (He rubs his eyes.) But I was watching your father, not the road.
SALMA: The police will believe you. You're older.
RASHID: (turning the officer's notepad toward her) Then you write it. Your words, not mine.
(Salma hesitates, then writes. Rashid reads over her shoulder and, where she pauses, quietly tells her the date.)
SALMA: You're not going to change it?
RASHID: (shaking his head) Your father taught me to trust what a careful person sees.
(A nurse crosses with a tray of tea glasses that rattle softly.)

[질문] Based on the scene, which choice best describes the relationship between Rashid and Salma?
A) Salma relies on Rashid to speak for her because she fears the police.
B) Rashid trusts Salma's judgment enough to set his own account aside.
C) Salma defers to Rashid's account because he is the older witness.
D) Rashid acts as a strict guardian who must approve what Salma says.
### lit40-medium-01-034 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다
[지문]
Years later, I still think about the back room of the tailor's shop in Valparaíso, where Benedita took over my lessons after my first teacher retired. She kept his chalk marks on the cutting table and never mentioned that his chair was empty. For weeks I answered her in single words and checked her stitches against his patterns when she wasn't looking. Then one afternoon she handed me his worn tape measure and asked me to show her how he had held it. I showed her, and she copied my grip exactly, without correcting me once. After that I began arriving early to sweep the threads before she came. Through the small window, cable cars climbed the hill, swaying above the painted roofs.

[질문] Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Dariush and Benedita?
A) Dariush resents Benedita for replacing a teacher whom he admired.
B) Benedita relies on Dariush to teach her a trade she does not know.
C) Dariush comes to trust Benedita because she honors his old teacher.

### lit40-medium-01-035 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다
[지문]
On the Monday the rumor reached Themba, I was waiting for the 6:40 bus under the shelter at the foot of the mountain. Someone had told him I was planning to sublet my flat to strangers and disappear, which was not true. I expected a letter, or a raised rent. Instead he sat down beside me on the bench, handed me half of his breakfast roll still warm in its paper, and said only, 'People talk. I told them you have lived in my building longer than my own sons.' When the bus came, he stood and waved it down for me, as if I could not do it myself. Mist was pouring over the ridge, soft as smoke, and the road shone wet below it.

[질문] Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Themba and Thandiwe?

### lit40-medium-01-036 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다

### lit40-medium-01-037 — skill inferences · 유형 relationship_between_characters · 요청 난이도 medium · hard 기준: 두 문장의 단서를 연결해야 하고 오답은 한쪽 감정만 반영한다
[지문]
A cracked clay jar lay at the bottom of the salt-water pool, where Alonso had dropped it while showing off for the fishermen's boys. In the old tellings, a jar that breaks in the sea keeps the voice of whoever broke it. Alonso's grandmother, Imtiaz, listened as he explained that a wave had knocked it from his hands. She did not scold him. She only waded in, lifted the shards, and held one to his ear. 'What does it say?' she asked. Alonso listened a long time. 'It says I was being foolish,' he admitted, and she pressed the shard into his palm as if he had earned it. Along the seawall, crows quarreled over a fish head in the noon glare.

[질문] Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Imtiaz and Alonso?

### lit40-medium-01-038 — skill inferences · 유형 symbolism · 요청 난이도 medium
[지문]
Radek tied the best knots in the building. Every Thursday at the corner laundromat, he bound the neighbors' laundry bags with a sailor's hitch, quick and neat, and every Thursday they stopped to admire it. 'A work of art,' Dmitri said, watching him cinch a bowline around a sack of towels. 'You should charge for that.' Radek only laughed. Later, when the dryers had finished, Dmitri saw the women at the folding table slip the knots loose with a single tug and toss the cords into the bin, still praising them as they left. Radek gathered the cords one by one and coiled them in his coat pocket. By the next Thursday he had tied them all again, as carefully as before. The machines thumped and turned behind the steamy windows.

[질문] In the passage, the knots most likely represent which of the following?

### lit40-medium-01-039 — skill inferences · 유형 symbolism · 요청 난이도 medium

Bologna had flooded twice that spring, and the cellar still held a skin of brown water when Meera went down for the wedding linens. Her daughter followed with a torch. Near the stairs floated a paper crown, soft at the edges, its gold paint bleeding into the water. Meera lifted it out before her daughter could. Years ago, at six, the girl had made her promise to wear exactly that crown at the wedding, whoever the groom turned out to be. Upstairs, they spread the linens across chairs to dry and found every one of them ruined. The crown, pressed flat between two dictionaries, kept most of its shape. 'Marco will think we're mad,' her daughter said, but she was already testing it against her own hair. Rain began again on the courtyard tiles.

### lit40-medium-01-040 — skill inferences · 유형 symbolism · 요청 난이도 medium
[지문]
Smell of cut grass and the harbor's salt,
and a ball thudding off the far goalpost.
Okja sits on the bleacher's lowest step,
her mother's medicine in a paper bag.

The boys kick it high, past the chalk line,
past the fence, toward the road to Seoul,
and every time it bounces back,
fetched by someone smaller, running home.

She has packed a bag twice this year.
Twice she has unpacked it by morning.

When the ball rolls to her shoes at last,
she holds it for a while, feels its weight,
then tosses it gently back onto the field.
The floodlights blink on, one bank at a time,
and gulls drift low across the stands.

A) Okja's urge to leave, which keeps bringing her back home
B) The carefree childhood that Okja wishes she could return to

### lit40-medium-01-041 — skill inferences · 유형 symbolism · 요청 난이도 medium

Why does a man wear a hat indoors? My daughter, Priya, asked this of Mayor Marlon one wet afternoon in the drying shed of the tea estate above Surabaya, where I had come, as the town's only doctor, to discuss the fever in the pickers' quarters. Marlon laughed and tipped the wide straw brim lower. He told me the clinic would get its new beds after the harvest, the same promise he had made after the last harvest. Each time I pressed him on the numbers, he adjusted the hat, and its shadow slid across his eyes like a shutter. Later, walking down between the rows, Priya said she thought he must have been cold. I told her yes, perhaps. But I had noticed that when the estate owner arrived in his car, Marlon took the hat off at once and held it against his chest, his face suddenly bare and eager.

Camryn had travelled with him that spring; you have always held him half to blame. Now he rests his hand upon the empty chair as he speaks, the way a man steadies himself against a rail. ### lit40-medium-01-043 — skill inferences · 유형 symbolism · 요청 난이도 medium

Three rules governed the old weaving house in Lisbon, and you learned them on your first day: no lamp after midnight, no cloth cut before it is finished, and no news spoken until it is certain. Rafaela, who had bought the house that winter, kept all three. Each morning she climbed to the loom room while Mateo, the gardener, pruned the lemon trees below, and each morning she wove one more row of a blue cloth with no pattern anyone could name. The ship carrying her brother was weeks overdue. When Mateo asked why she did not weave something useful, a shawl or a blanket, she only said that the cloth was not finished. Rows gathered like days. Once, when a rumor of a wreck came up the hill, her hands stopped above the threads for a full hour; then she tied the next knot and went on. By midsummer, Mateo had begun bringing her a sprig of lemon blossom each dawn and laying it, without a word, beside the growing blue.

### lit40-medium-01-044 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 medium

Years later, Rangi would still remember the evening his son refused to leave the gymnasium in Lyon. It was the anniversary of Elodie's death, and Rangi had planned a quiet dinner at the restaurant she had loved. The boy, fourteen and immovable, had other ideas: he wanted to shoot free throws in the empty gym where his mother had once coached, one for every year since she had been gone. Rangi argued, then pleaded, then sat on the bottom bleacher with his coat still buttoned. His son did not answer. ### lit40-medium-01-045 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 medium

Night is honest. In the sanatorium above the lake outside Bergen, I learned that patients say at two in the morning what they hide by daylight. Thorvald, my night patient, could not sleep unless I wheeled him to the end of the dock, where the water lay black and still. On the fourth night he showed me an envelope addressed to his brother, sealed and stamped and eleven years old. He had written it the week after their quarrel. He never mailed it, he said, and his brother had died the following spring. He held it on his blanket while he talked, and I understood that the apology had become an anchor he dragged behind him, slowing every hour he had left. Before dawn he asked me, Sigrid, to keep it for him. I put it in my apron pocket, where it weighed almost nothing.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “an anchor he dragged behind him” most nearly suggests that the unsent apology was
A) a source of steadiness that kept Thorvald calm at night
B) a memory Thorvald was ready to throw into the lake
C) a hope of reconciliation that still guided his choices
D) a weight of regret that kept holding Thorvald back
### lit40-medium-01-046 — skill words_in_context · 유형 figurative_language · 요청 난이도 medium
[지문]
Who pays a clockmaker for the hours he gives away?
My father, Santiago, bent above his bench
on Forty-Third Street, where the trains shook dust
from the rafters into every open case.
Ottavio came in winter with a watch
his wife had worn, its mainspring broken, its glass
clouded like a frozen pond.
He counted out his nickels on the counter.
My father pushed them back without a word
and worked past closing, past supper, past the lamps,
spending his minutes like coins on a stranger
while I translated nothing, for nothing needed saying.
When the watch ticked, Ottavio wept in Italian.
My father answered him in Spanish.
I stood between them with my English,
the only one who thought words were required.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “spending his minutes like coins on a stranger” most nearly suggests that Santiago was
A) giving his own time freely in place of taking payment
B) wasting time carelessly on a repair he did not value
C) charging Ottavio for every minute of his labor
D) hurrying to finish the repair so he could close
